name: Yellow.ai
tagline: A $500M-valuation enterprise conversational AI platform spanning 35+ channels and 135+ languages, serving Sony and Volkswagen — with real, specific complaints about pricing opacity and WhatsApp number lock-in.
tldr: Yellow.ai (formerly Yellow Messenger) was founded in 2016 in Bangalore by Raghu Ravinutala, Jaya Kishore Reddy Gollareddy, and Rashid Khan, has raised $356.6M+ across five rounds reaching a $500M valuation in 2021, and now serves 1,300+ enterprises including Sony, Domino's, Hyundai, Volkswagen, and Papa Johns across 85+ countries.

Scale is the clearest differentiator: 35+ voice and text channels and 135+ languages, both figures well beyond any other tool reviewed in this category — this is closer to a full enterprise conversational-AI platform than a WhatsApp-focused tool.

Pricing is entirely opaque and sales-quoted — AWS Marketplace listings reference $10,000/year for a Basic contract and $25,000/year for Standard, with typical custom Enterprise deals starting around $50,000+/year, plus per-resolution fees and professional-services costs for implementation.

Real, specific, and serious complaints recur across independent reviews: pricing opacity and cost escalation as more channels get added, poor support communication with reported high staff turnover, difficulty modifying a live automation workflow once built, and — most concerning — at least one review describing the company as making it 'very cumbersome to migrate' away because it holds the customer's WhatsApp number.

A documented NLP weakness shows up specifically in reviews: the bot is described as losing context and not always doing a good job at intent matching, which can create more work for human agents rather than less.

Best for large enterprises with genuine multi-channel, multi-language conversational AI needs and the internal resources to manage a complex, sales-negotiated vendor relationship — not for small-to-mid businesses, or anyone wanting transparent, predictable pricing.
keyFeatures: Dynamic AI Agents delivering conversational automation across 35+ voice and text channels and 135+ languages
One-click Salesforce CRM integration that pushes leads and information collected by chatbots and voice bots directly into Salesforce
Salesforce state-change event listening, triggering real-time notifications to business stakeholders on channels like WhatsApp and SMS
Shopify storefront connection for AI agents, documented as a few-click setup
AI-first voice automation connecting with contact center solutions and IVR systems
Enterprise-grade workflow builder for constructing multi-step conversational journeys across channels
HubSpot and other CRM/business-system integrations alongside the deeper Salesforce implementation
A sales-negotiated Enterprise tier with professional services support for large-scale, multi-channel deployments

faq.question: How does Yellow.ai's pricing actually work?
faq.answer: It's entirely custom and sales-quoted — no public pricing page exists. AWS Marketplace listings reference $10,000/year for a Basic contract and $25,000/year for Standard, and typical custom Enterprise deals are reported starting around $50,000+/year, with per-resolution fees and professional-services implementation costs on top. Independent reviews specifically describe cost escalating past the original contract scope as more channels get added — budget for growth, not just the initial quote.

faq.question: Is it hard to leave Yellow.ai once you've signed up?
faq.answer: At least one independent reviewer specifically raises this as a serious concern, stating the company 'holds your WhatsApp number and make[s] it very cumbersome to migrate to anyone else.' If WhatsApp is a core channel for your business, understand exactly how number portability and account ownership work in your contract before signing, not after you're already dependent on the platform.

faq.question: How many channels and languages does Yellow.ai actually support?
faq.answer: 35+ voice and text channels and 135+ languages, both figures substantially larger than any other tool in this comparison category. This scale is the platform's clearest strength and the reason it's positioned as an enterprise conversational-AI platform rather than a channel-specific tool like most WhatsApp-focused competitors.

faq.question: How reliable is Yellow.ai's AI at understanding customer intent?
faq.answer: Independent reviewers specifically describe the bot losing context and not always doing a good job at intent matching, which can create more work for human agents rather than less — a genuine, documented weakness rather than a vague quality complaint. Test this directly against your own real customer conversations before assuming enterprise-grade NLP performance out of the box.

faq.question: What's the most common complaint about Yellow.ai's support?
faq.answer: Poor support communication is one of the most frequently repeated complaints in independent reviews, with users specifically describing 'horrible communication' and citing high staff turnover as a contributing factor. Given the platform's enterprise scale and sales-negotiated contracts, this is worth probing directly with current customer references before signing a multi-year agreement.

faq.question: Can I easily update a live automation workflow after building it?
faq.answer: Not easily, according to independent reviews — building a new conversational journey is described as straightforward, but modifying one that's already live reads as an engineering task rather than a simple edit. Factor this into your evaluation if your use case requires frequent iteration on live customer-facing flows.

What makes this more than a typical 'contact sales' inconvenience is the specific, repeated independent-review pattern describing cost escalation: a scoped project growing meaningfully in price once additional channels get added after the initial contract. Combined with the documented WhatsApp-number lock-in complaint, this is a vendor relationship where getting exact multi-year cost projections, channel-addition pricing, and account-portability terms in writing before signing matters more than with almost any other tool in this category.

None of these are typical vendor grumbling — they're specific, credible operational risks.

verdict: Yellow.ai's scale is genuinely exceptional and not marketing exaggeration — 35+ channels and 135+ languages is a real, substantial technical achievement that no other tool in this comparison category comes close to matching, and the customer roster (Sony, Domino's, Hyundai, Volkswagen) confirms this works at real enterprise scale. The Salesforce integration is similarly sophisticated: one-click setup with real-time event-listening that pushes bot-collected data into the CRM and routes notifications back out, deeper than most competitors' CRM connections. But the honest, necessary counterweight to that scale is a specific, credible, and repeated pattern of operational risk in independent reviews that goes well beyond typical vendor grumbling. Pricing is entirely opaque and sales-negotiated, with documented cost escalation as more channels get added after the initial contract. Support communication is repeatedly described as poor, with high staff turnover cited as a contributing factor. And most seriously, at least one reviewer describes the company holding a customer's WhatsApp number in a way that makes leaving 'very cumbersome' — a genuine lock-in risk, not a hypothetical one. Layer on documented, specific complaints about the AI losing context and struggling with intent matching, and the picture is a platform whose raw capability ceiling is genuinely high but whose real-world execution carries real, specific risks that a large enterprise buyer needs to negotiate around explicitly, not discover after signing. My honest read: if you're a large enterprise with genuine need for Yellow.ai's channel and language breadth, this is worth evaluating seriously — but insist on explicit written terms for cost escalation, WhatsApp number portability, and support SLAs before committing, and pilot the AI against your own real conversations to test the documented intent-matching concerns directly.
